title: Violin Concerto No. 1 in A minor
hook: Bach takes the Italian concerto he learned from Vivaldi and makes it his own, ending with a jig that shimmers across the violin’s strings.

painting.title: Regatta on the Grand Canal in Honor of Frederick IV, King of Denmark
painting.collection: The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
painting.pairingNote: Venice in festival dress, painted in 1711, the year Vivaldi’s first great set of violin concertos was published; the Italian concerto that Bach copied, arranged and then made his own in this work.

facts: No one knows exactly when Bach wrote it. The only source in his hand is a set of parts copied in Leipzig around 1730 by Bach, his son Carl Philipp Emanuel, his pupil Johann Ludwig Krebs and another copyist. For a long time it was thought to come from his years at Köthen (1717–23), where he led the prince’s small orchestra; some scholars now think he wrote it for the Collegium Musicum, the Leipzig concert society he took over in 1729.

Bach learned the concerto from Vivaldi. In Weimar, around 1713–14, he arranged a number of Vivaldi’s violin concertos for keyboard and organ. This one follows the Italian plan: three movements, fast–slow–fast, with a returning band refrain, the [[ritornello|ritornello]], in the outer movements. But Bach weaves the band and the soloist far more tightly together.

Bach was a violinist himself. His son Carl Philipp Emanuel later wrote that his father played the violin “cleanly and penetratingly” until late in life. Later Bach arranged this concerto for harpsichord, a tone lower, in G minor (BWV 1058).

It never quite dropped out of sight. In 1841 Felix Mendelssohn passed the score to Ferdinand David, leader of the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra, and it was first printed in 1852. Not everyone was won over: after its first American performance, in 1860, a critic called it “very heavy and uninspired”.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a fierce, purposeful A minor (I), a slow song over a rolling bass (II), a quick jig (III).

movements.heading: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: The band opens with a firm, assertive theme, the [[ritornello|ritornello]], which comes back in fragments and in new keys throughout the movement. When the violin enters it brings its own, more yearning idea. The two characters alternate and overlap until the opening theme returns in A minor to close.

mainIdeas.name: The ritornello
mainIdeas.description: a bold, purposeful theme for the band, starting with a short, emphatic figure and running on in quick notes.

mainIdeas.name: The violin’s theme
mainIdeas.description: a longer, more lyrical, yearning line that the band never takes over.

stops.hear: The strings set out a firm, purposeful theme in A minor
The solo violin enters with a more yearning line; the band drops back to accompany
The band’s theme returns, brighter, in a major key
The violin moves through darker keys in quick, flowing passages; pieces of the band’s theme keep breaking in
stops.happening: Solo episodes, interlocked with the ritornello

stops.hear: The opening theme, back in A minor, for everyone

notice: Listen for the two characters: the band’s assertive theme and the violin’s longing one. They share the movement, but each keeps its own material.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Hilary Hahn plays on a modern violin with the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra, conducted by Jeffrey Kahane; the recording was made in Los Angeles in January 2003. On the Spotify album this concerto is tracks 7–9, after the E major concerto and the Double Concerto.

movements.heading: Andante
movements.summary: A slow movement in C major built over a short, insistent figure in the bass that comes back again and again, while the harmony above it changes. Over it the violin sings a long, free line, almost like an opera aria. Only in the last phrase do bass, band and soloist come together.

mainIdeas.name: The bass figure
mainIdeas.description: a short, rolling pattern in the cellos and bass, repeated through the movement, an [[ostinato|ostinato]].

mainIdeas.name: The violin’s song
mainIdeas.description: long, decorated phrases above, sometimes soaring, sometimes almost speaking.

stops.hear: The cellos and bass play a short, rolling figure; soft chords answer above
stops.happening: The [[ostinato|ostinato]] that runs through the movement

stops.hear: The solo violin enters with a long, singing line over the figure
stops.happening: The song begins, in C major

stops.hear: The music turns to minor keys; the violin’s line grows more intense while the bass figure keeps returning
stops.happening: The emotional centre of the movement

stops.hear: The music finds its way back towards C major

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: The violin and the band finally join in one phrase, then a quiet close
stops.happening: Everything comes together at the end

notice: Follow the bass for a minute. The same short figure returns again and again, in different keys, underneath the violin’s song.

movements.heading: Allegro assai
movements.summary: A fast jig in nine quick beats to the bar, grouped in threes. Each time the band plays its refrain, the instruments enter one after another as in a [[fugue|fugue]]. Between these entries the soloist races in brilliant passages, and near the end the violin rocks rapidly between two strings, one of them left open, so that a single line seems to shimmer.

mainIdeas.name: The jig theme
mainIdeas.description: a bouncing, skipping tune in threes, passed from part to part in the band.

mainIdeas.name: The solo passages
mainIdeas.description: quick runs and, near the end, a rapid rocking across the strings.

stops.hear: A bouncing jig tune in the first violins, then the other parts entering one by one
stops.happening: The ritornello, built as a fugue

stops.hear: The solo violin breaks away in quick, brilliant passages
The jig tune in the band again, in another key, the parts entering one by one
stops.happening: The ritornello in a new key

stops.hear: The violin races through a long solo while the band supports lightly

stops.hear: The jig tune for the full band, back in A minor

notice: Near the end, listen for the moment the violin’s line turns into a fast, glittering flicker between two notes. It is one player rocking the bow across two strings.

threads.title: From Vivaldi to Bach
threads.body: The plan is Italian: fast–slow–fast, a returning refrain, a virtuoso soloist. What is Bach’s own is the counterpoint: fugal entries in the finale and a bass that never stops working in the Andante.

threads.title: A violinist’s concerto
threads.body: Bach knew the instrument from the inside: the yearning solo line of the first movement, the long song of the second and the string-crossing effects of the third are all written for the violin’s own strengths.

threads.title: The same music, another instrument
threads.body: Bach later turned it into a harpsichord concerto in G minor. Hearing that version shows how much of the violin part he had to rewrite for the keyboard.
